items.title: Eddie Palmieri — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He’s the one, the musical director of Machito, his brother-in-law, and introduces Chano Pozo, in 1947-1948, to Dizzy Gillespie.

ctx.x: Well, let’s go back to talking about Mario Bauzá.

He’s the one, the musical director of Machito, his brother-in-law, and introduces Chano Pozo, in 1947-1948, to Dizzy Gillespie. Then Dizzy, in an interview, said, “Chano didn’t speak English, I didn’t speak Spanish, but we both spoke African.” [LAUGHS]
Thank you so much for helping the audience to understand this development of the roots of what we call now “Latin Music.”

items.title: 61124_Mario Bauza oral history interview
items.q: Why? Because every time they -- Eddie sit down at a piano to play that, he find faults with the orchestra.

ctx.x: And all the arrangements Rene made for the album for Columbia, he came here, they couldn't get no (unintelligible) they couldn't record it. They went back to Puerto Rico and they got to go after a three-day in the studio and the week after Rene died. So they didn't record none of that. Why? Because every time they -- Eddie sit down at a piano to play that, he find faults with the orchestra. (Unintelligible.)
Of course, Rene Alandos had a lot to do with Benito, didn't he?
